grinder_families.name: Conical burrs
grinder_families.description: Conical burr sets (most hand grinders and many home electric grinders).
notes: Conicals are on average less unimodal and less uniform than flat burrs, with large overlap between models (Gagné 2023, grade D). Family values are judgements; calibrate with your own shots.

sources.citation: Gagné J. (2023) What I learned from analyzing 300 particle size distributions for 24 espresso grinders. Coffee ad Astra.

grinder_families.name: Flat burrs, traditional geometry
grinder_families.description: Conventional flat espresso burrs (most commercial and prosumer flat grinders).
notes: Family values are judgements anchored on the Bentwood V63 (Smrke 2024), the EK43 (Cameron 2020) and a disc grinder (Corrochano 2017); calibrate with your own shots.

sources.citation: Gagné J. (2023) What I learned from analyzing 300 particle size distributions for 24 espresso grinders. Coffee ad Astra.
Smrke S., Eiermann A., Yeretzian C. (2024) The role of fines in espresso extraction dynamics. Sci. Rep. 14:5612.
Roman Corrochano B. (2017) Advancing the engineering understanding of coffee extraction. EngD thesis, University of Birmingham.

grinder_families.name: Flat burrs, unimodal (low-fines) geometry
grinder_families.description: Flat burrs designed for a narrow, low-fines distribution (e.g. "unimodal", "high uniformity" or "ultra low fines" burr sets). Fewer fines at a given median; such grinders need a finer median to reach the same shot time.
notes: Family values are judgements from Gagné 2023's qualitative comparison of 24 grinders (grade D); calibrate with your own shots.
Unimodal burrs are dialled in by the amount of fines more than by the median (03 §2.1): expect a much finer setting than with traditional burrs.

sources.citation: Gagné J. (2023) What I learned from analyzing 300 particle size distributions for 24 espresso grinders. Coffee ad Astra.
Gagné J. (2021) A comparison between standard and low-fines espresso shots. Coffee ad Astra.

grinders.name: AMZCHEF single-dose grinder
grinders.description: Single-dose electric grinder, listed with 40 mm conical burrs, stepless adjustment with about 75 marked settings, roughly 450 rpm and under 0.2 g retention. All listing specifications are UNVERIFIED; the dial mapping is a guess to be calibrated.
notes: UNVERIFIED: 40 mm conical burrs, about 75 marked settings (stepless) and ~450 rpm come from retail listings only (PLAN §15).

Estimated dial mapping, a wide prior: gap = 50 µm + 15 µm per marked setting (plausible ranges 0–150 µm and 8–25 µm per setting). Log a few shots (dose, yield, time, gauge pressure) to calibrate it, or set grinder.gap_at_ref_um and grinder.gap_per_unit_um.

Lower settings are assumed finer, with espresso around settings 5–15. The default (10, X50 ≈ 280 µm) is placed where published espresso grinds lie by particle size (X50 ≈ 200–360 µm by dry laser diffraction or image analysis: Smrke 2024, Cameron 2020, Corrochano 2017), not from shot times; settings 0–3 give Turkish-like grinds (X50 ≈ 70–110 µm).

sources.citation: Retail and aggregator listings for the AMZCHEF single-dose coffee grinder (accessed 2026-10-13; no manufacturer page confirmed them).
Puckworks input models (2026), docs/model/input-models.md: dial mapping estimated, to be calibrated.

grinders.name: Bentwood Vertical 63
grinders.description: 63 mm flat burrs with a dial calibrated in micrometres of burr spacing. The best-anchored grinder: X50 and fines were measured at six spacings (Smrke 2024).
notes: X50 ≈ 1.4 × burr spacing was measured over 160–250 µm with a Camsizer X2 (projected-area size, x_area); outside that range the relation is extrapolated.
Fines (volume % below 100 µm) follow the model's fines relation with u_G = 15.7% at X50 = 340 µm, fitted to Smrke 2024's six spacings (within 0.3 points of Q100 at the measured medians).

sources.citation: Smrke S., Eiermann A., Yeretzian C. (2024) The role of fines in espresso extraction dynamics. Sci. Rep. 14:5612.

grinders.name: Generic 50 mm conical burrs
grinders.description: A typical home conical grinder (electric or hand); set the burr gap directly.
notes: The setting is the burr gap in µm. Burr diameter and rpm are recorded but have no systematic effect in the evidence (03 §2.1).

The default gap puts X50 at about 240–270 µm, where published espresso grinds lie by particle size (X50 ≈ 200–360 µm: Smrke 2024, Cameron 2020, Corrochano 2017); it is not derived from shot times. Gaps below about 100 µm give Turkish-like grinds.
Hand grinders often state µm per click (e.g. 8.8 µm for a 1Zpresso J-Max, 03 §2.2); multiply your clicks from burr contact by that step to get the gap.

sources.citation: Gagné J. (2023) What I learned from analyzing 300 particle size distributions for 24 espresso grinders. Coffee ad Astra.
1Zpresso. J-series specifications.

grinders.name: Mahlkönig E65S
grinders.description: 65 mm flat steel burrs, 1400 rpm (50 Hz; 1700 rpm at 60 Hz), 80-indicator dial. The grinder of the Schmieder 2023 extraction-kinetics study; its dial is mapped to a burr gap so that the model reproduces the measured volume mean diameters at grind levels 1.4 and 2.0.
notes: Disputed dial scale: the brochure's 180–580 µm over 80 indicators (≈5 µm per indicator) is read as burr movement in note 03 but as a particle-size bandwidth by Schmieder 2023. Neither reading is used directly: the mapping (25 µm of gap per grind-level unit, i.e. 2.5 µm per indicator) is fitted to the measured D43 of 273 µm at GL 1.4 and 295 µm at GL 2.0.
Measured D43 values are by wet laser diffraction (SD 8–18 µm). Wet D32 (27–29 µm) includes 1–10 µm debris; the model's Sauter diameter is dry-equivalent and much larger.
Dial steps of interest (GL 1.4–2.0) are near the repeatability of PSD measurements (03 §2.2).

sources.citation: Schmieder B.K.L., Pannusch V.B., Vannieuwenhuyse L., Briesen H., Minceva M. (2023) Influence of flow rate, particle size, and temperature on espresso extraction kinetics. Foods 12:2871.
Mahlkönig/Hemro. E65S product brochure (DE).

grinders.name: Mahlkönig EK43 (coffee burrs)
grinders.description: 98 mm flat burrs at 1480 rpm with the stock coffee burrs. Espresso is typically ground at settings 1.0–2.5; extraction peaks near 1.7 (Cameron 2020). The dial is arbitrary (zero where the burrs chirp); its mapping is fitted to Cameron 2020's measured particle sizes.
notes: Dial mapping fitted to Cameron 2020's laser-diffraction PSDs at settings 1.0–2.5 (X50 205–360 µm, dispersion not stated): an effective gap of 72 µm + 71 µm per unit, i.e. X50 ≈ 1.4 × (72 + 71 × setting) µm, within 6% of the measured medians. Fines: u_G = 16.1% (Q100 within 1.1 points).
Below setting 1.0 the mapping is extrapolated; at 0 (burrs chirping) it gives X50 ≈ 100 µm, the finest this grinder reaches in the model.

Roast offset: at the same setting a dark roast grinds finer; light at 2.0 matched dark at 2.3 (Méndez Harper 2024). The bean model's roast factor (model.psd.roast_coefficient) reproduces this shift with this mapping.

sources.citation: Cameron M.I., Morisco D., Hofstetter D., Uman E., Wilkinson J., Kennedy Z.C., Fontenot S.A., Lee W.T., Hendon C.H., Foster J.M. (2020) Systematically improving espresso: insights from mathematical modeling and experiment. Matter 2:631–648.
Méndez Harper J. et al. (2024; online 2023) Moisture-controlled triboelectrification during coffee grinding. Matter 7:1–18.

machines.name: Allongé
machines.description: A long, very coarse shot at 4.5 mL/s with pressure capped at 6 bar (profiling pump).
notes: Allongé shots use a very coarse grind and a 1:4–1:5 ratio; the flow and pressure cap are typical, not from a published protocol.

machines.name: AMZCHEF Ultra
machines.description: Home espresso machine with a 58 mm portafilter, a vibratory pump sold as "20 bar", a pressure gauge and a PID set from 88 to 96 °C. Pump curve and over-pressure valve are unknown.
notes: Owner confirmed: 58 mm single-wall basket and pressure gauge (PLAN D10; basket type confirmed 2026-10-15). Basket depth, taper and open area remain estimated.
UNVERIFIED: "20 bar" pump and PID range 88–96 °C come from retail listings only (PLAN §15).

UNKNOWN pump curve and over-pressure valve: estimated as 8 mL/s free flow and 17 bar stall, with no OPV. If the gauge never rises above a fixed value during a choked shot, that value is the OPV: set machine.pump.opv_bar.
The gauge of such machines may read pump pressure rather than pressure at the puck.

UNVERIFIED: no three-way valve assumed (many budget vibratory machines lack one), so the water above the puck drips into the cup after the stop. If the machine hisses into the drip tray at the stop and leaves a dry puck, it has one: set machine.vent_headspace to true.
The default 58 mm stock double represents the owner's confirmed single-wall basket.

sources.citation: Project owner (2026-10-15): confirmed 58 mm single-wall basket; pressure gauge confirmed 2026-10-14 (PLAN D10).
Retail and aggregator listings for the AMZCHEF Ultra espresso machine (accessed 2026-10-13; no manufacturer page confirmed them).

machines.name: Blooming espresso
machines.description: Fill at 4 mL/s until about 3.5 bar, pause 20 s with the pump off while the puck soaks, then extract at up to 9 bar with the flow capped at 3 mL/s (profiling pump).
notes: Timings are typical of blooming programs on profiling machines, not from a published protocol.

machines.name: Declining 9 → 6 bar
machines.description: 9 bar for 8 s, then a linear decline to 6 bar over 15 s, held to the end (profiling pump).
notes: A common profiling shape; the timings are typical, not from a published protocol.

sources.citation: Puckworks input models (2026), docs/model/input-models.md: typical program, estimated.

machines.name: Rotary pump, E61-style group
machines.description: A rotary pump with its bypass set to about 9 bar (a nearly constant-pressure source) feeding a heavy E61-style group, whose mechanical pre-infusion chamber softens the pressure rise.
notes: The flow restrictor (gicleur) caps the flow, here at 6 mL/s; the pre-infusion chamber is approximated by a 4 s pressure ramp. Both are estimates.
E61-style groups have a three-way solenoid valve that vents the group at the stop, so no headspace water drips into the cup.

sources.citation: Puckworks input models (2026), docs/model/input-models.md: typical machine, estimated.

machines.name: Flat 9 bar
machines.description: Constant 9 bar at the puck from a profiling (ideal) pump, after a 2 s ramp.
notes: An ideal pump holds the programmed pressure exactly, within its flow limit (8 mL/s by default).

sources.citation: Ellero M., Navarini L. (2019) Mesoscopic modelling and simulation of espresso coffee extraction. J. Food Eng. 263:181–194.

machines.name: Flow profile, 2 mL/s
machines.description: Constant 2 mL/s from a flow-controlled pump, with pressure capped at 10 bar.
notes: At 2 mL/s the headspace fills slowly, so the first drops come later than with a pressure profile.

sources.citation: Schmieder B.K.L., Pannusch V.B., Vannieuwenhuyse L., Briesen H., Minceva M. (2023) Influence of flow rate, particle size, and temperature on espresso extraction kinetics. Foods 12:2871.

machines.name: Spring lever
machines.description: Pre-infusion at boiler pressure while the lever is held down, then the spring pushes the piston: a peak near 9 bar that declines as the spring extends.
notes: A spring lever's pressure falls with piston travel, i.e. with the volume dispensed; here it falls linearly with time (9 → 4.5 bar over 22 s), an approximation.
Pre-infusion at about 1.2 bar of boiler pressure for 8 s; peak and decline values are typical, not measured on a particular machine.
Lever groups have no three-way valve: the water above the puck drips into the cup after the stop.

sources.citation: Puckworks input models (2026), docs/model/input-models.md: typical program, estimated.

machines.name: Turbo shot, 6 bar
machines.description: 6 bar with a high flow cap, for coarse "turbo" shots (about 15 s at a 1:3 ratio); lower pressure avoided the clogging Cameron 2020 saw at 9 bar with fine grinds.
notes: Grind much coarser than for a 9 bar shot and use a longer ratio (about 1:3).

sources.citation: Cameron M.I., Morisco D., Hofstetter D., Uman E., Wilkinson J., Kennedy Z.C., Fontenot S.A., Lee W.T., Hendon C.H., Foster J.M. (2020) Systematically improving espresso: insights from mathematical modeling and experiment. Matter 2:631–648.

machines.name: Vibratory pump, no profiling
machines.description: A typical home machine: a vibratory pump at full power on its pump curve, with an over-pressure valve (OPV) at 12 bar.
notes: Linear pump curve with registry defaults (9 mL/s free flow, 16 bar stall) and an OPV at 12 bar: typical values, not a particular pump. A gauge reading during a shot calibrates them.
No three-way valve assumed: many budget vibratory machines lack one, but others have it (it hisses into the drip tray at the stop and leaves a dry puck); then set machine.vent_headspace to true.

sources.citation: Puckworks input models (2026), docs/model/input-models.md: typical vibratory pump, estimated.
